Fantasy is a literary and imaginative genre that presents worlds, beings, and events governed by magical or supernatural principles rather than physical laws. Distinct from science fiction, which extrapolates from known science, and from magical realism, which embeds magic in our world, fantasy constructs complete alternate worlds with their own internal coherence.

As a mode of storytelling, fantasy privileges wonder, enchantment, and the possible over the probable. Although fantastical tales are ancient—myth, legend, and fairy tales predate the modern category—fantasy as a formal literary genre solidified in the twentieth century. The modern category lacks the self-aware genre consciousness of those ancient forms.

Central to modern fantasy theory is the concept of the secondary world: a complete imaginative universe with its own rules, geography, and history. The reader enters it fully, suspending disbelief at the threshold. Magic systems in modern fantasy can be hard-defined, governed by rules with costs and limitations, or soft and mysterious, poetic and less mechanistic. The writer's choice reflects their philosophical approach to wonder.

Epic or high fantasy typically features a struggle between good and evil across a detailed world. Urban or contemporary fantasy, by contrast, relocates magic to the modern present, grounding the marvelous in familiar geography. Fantasy allows exploration of psychological, moral, and spiritual themes through the distance and safety of the marvelous rather than the literal. Allegory and symbol operate freely within fantasy's logic.

The genre encompasses many subgenres: sword and sorcery, paranormal romance, cozy fantasy, portal fantasy, and others. This diversity reflects fantasy's capacity to absorb different narrative concerns and tones. The tradition traces back to J.R.R. Tolkien, who architected the modern literary fantasy world as a complete imaginative system. The Lord of the Rings became the canonical modern fantasy epic that defined the genre's narrative scope and aesthetic, influencing everything that came after.
